rules.statement: When a lookup by a key that is meant to identify exactly one record finds more than one match, return no result instead of picking one or throwing.
rules.why: Picking one could route a request to the wrong owner, and throwing would turn every request for that key into a server error because of one bad row; returning nothing fails closed as 'unknown'.
rules.check: Look for lookups that use FirstOrDefault/First or throw on multiple matches for keys that must be unique (e.g. a host used for routing); they should detect more than one match and return null/none.

rules.statement: Uniqueness validation must use a query that returns every current holder of the key, not the fail-closed routing lookup, so a key that is already ambiguous still counts as taken.
rules.why: A routing lookup that returns nothing on ambiguity would make a conflicting key look free and let a new write add another conflict.
rules.check: Check that write-time uniqueness checks call a list-all-holders query and reject the key when any other record holds it, rather than reusing a single-result lookup.

rules.statement: Compute a normalized, indexed lookup column from its source value on every write, and never let it be set on its own.
rules.why: Deriving it on write means the indexed value cannot drift from the value that is published.
rules.check: Look for normalized/derived columns (e.g. Normalized*Host) that are assigned from input or left unchanged when the source value changes; they must be recomputed from the source property on every write.

rules.statement: When a write leaves out an optional value that has a configuration-derived default, apply the default (`value ??= default`), validate the result, and store the derived value instead of resolving it at read time.
rules.why: A stored value does not move when configuration changes later, and validating after the default is applied checks the value that will actually be served.
rules.check: Look for defaults computed on read from configuration, or validation that runs before the default is applied; also check that clearing the value on update restores the derived default.

rules.statement: Validate configured URL templates and authorities used to build addresses at startup: check scheme, required placeholders, and that each expanded value is consistent with the routing rules.
rules.why: A bad template would otherwise give tenants addresses that cannot be routed or that collide, and the problem would only show up at request time.
rules.check: New configuration options holding URL templates or authorities should have startup (options) validation checking https scheme, required placeholders such as {tenantId} in the host, round-trip routing and non-collision with other templates.

rules.statement: Model a value that routes requests to exactly one tenant as a first-class, indexed tenant property, not as an inherited or merged setting.
rules.why: Routing needs an indexed lookup across tenants before any tenant is known, and an inherited value would route every tenant to the same place.
rules.check: Flag new per-tenant hosts, origins or routing keys added as merged/inherited settings instead of tenant properties with an index.

rules.statement: An RFC 8705 mTLS endpoint alias must be an `https` origin (scheme, host, optional port, no path), and its host must differ from the issuer's host.
rules.why: Endpoints are rewritten onto the alias origin, and one host cannot both ask for and skip a client certificate.
rules.check: Check that validation of mtls_endpoint_aliases authorities rejects non-https values, values with a path, and a host equal to the issuer host.

rules.statement: Every additional origin a tenant publishes (such as an mTLS endpoint alias) must pass the same host validation as the issuer: it must route back to that tenant, and no other tenant may serve it.
rules.why: Without this, a tenant could advertise endpoints it cannot serve, or collide with another tenant's host.
rules.check: When a published origin is added or changed, verify that host-pattern round-trip and cross-tenant uniqueness checks run on it, and that updates re-check the address when either the issuer or the alias changes.

rules.statement: The published `issuer` must stay the tenant's configured authoritative origin and must never be derived from the request host, even when the request arrives on an alias host.
rules.why: The issuer is the single authoritative origin that every published URL and token is anchored to; an alias is a second origin for endpoints only.
rules.check: Flag code that builds the issuer or token `iss` from HttpContext.Request.Host or the alias authority.
